buyer: 911 agencies and emergency communications centers first — the site claims 50,000+ first responder agencies and lists Law Enforcement, Fire/EMS, State Government, and Schools and Universities as public-safety segments — alongside 10,000+ enterprise partners in connected vehicles, fleets and telematics, rideshare and delivery (Uber is named), healthcare, retail, utilities, robotics and consumer devices.
note: This is a genuine two-sided business and the site says so: one nav branch is public safety (911 agencies, law enforcement, fire/EMS, state government, schools and universities) and the other is enterprise (OEMs and connected vehicles, autonomous vehicles and robotics, fleets/logistics/telematics, healthcare, retail, critical infrastructure and utilities, technology and platform partners). So a share of its roles will be selling into devices and enterprises rather than into agencies. Our category "EMS" fits the public-safety half; the product is emergency data routed into 911 centers rather than EMS clinical or billing software.

name: Eventeny
buyer: Event organizers who run festivals, fairs, conventions and community events — a genuinely mixed group that includes municipal and county governments (City of Suwanee, Deschutes County Fair, Wood County Fair) alongside private convention and festival companies (GalaxyCon, Fanatics Fest, Florida Renaissance Festival, Anime Milwaukee, Avalon Park Group) and chambers of commerce.
note: Their case studies page is where the public buyers show up by name: the City of Suwanee write-up says Suwanee hosts "40+ events yearly" on a paper-based system before Eventeny, and Deschutes County Fair and Wood County Fair are county entities. The homepage also lists City of Lawrenceville, City of Alpharetta and Michigan State Fair. Worth flagging: their /solutions/ page names no government buyer at all — it sells by event type ("Food & drink festivals", "Fandom conventions", "Pride events") rather than by buyer, so anyone checking only that page would miss the public-sector side entirely. Commercial side is unambiguous: DragonCon, Fanatics Fest and a private developer (Avalon Park Group) are named customers, so this is a dual-market vendor, not a gov-only one. Our "Events, Venues & Ticketing" category matches what the site sells.

name: Niche Technology
buyer: Police forces and law enforcement agencies exclusively — the site says it serves "174k+ Sworn officers in over 180 agencies worldwide" and names municipal, county and national police agencies as its entire customer base.
note: Every named customer is a police agency. US state-and-local ones include Kansas City Police Department, Springfield (Missouri) PD, Olathe (Kansas) PD, Temple (Texas) PD and Orange County, New York. The bulk of the named base is actually UK and Canadian — South Yorkshire Police, Durham Constabulary, Warwickshire Police, Hampshire Constabulary, North Wales Police, Merseyside Police, Toronto Police Service, Peel Regional Police, Ontario Provincial Police, Regina Police Service. Those are still public buyers but not US SLED, so the US SLED footprint is a minority of the customer list even though the company is 100% government-facing. No corrections, school, private-security or commercial buyer appears anywhere. Their /who-we-serve/ page renders its agency list through an interactive map that did not return names to a fetch; the homepage carried the named agencies instead. Our "Police" category is exactly right.

name: K16 Solutions
buyer: Higher education institutions — universities, colleges, community colleges and multi-campus university systems, sold to campus IT leadership that owns the LMS and the data layer.
note: The named customer wall is entirely colleges and universities: UCLA, UC Riverside, San Diego State, Texas Tech, University at Buffalo, UMass Amherst, Boise State, Collin College, Monroe Community College, Kean University, Arkansas State, Southern University System, University of Louisiana System, Seton Hall, USC, University of Tampa, Meharry Medical College. Under the house rule that universities and colleges are public buyers whether public or private, that makes sells_outside_government "no" — but the reasoning is worth stating rather than hiding, because several of those (USC, Seton Hall, University of Tampa) are private institutions and three more (De Montfort, University of Manchester, VU Amsterdam) are foreign universities, so the base is narrower in US-public terms than the raw count suggests. The site explicitly targets "Higher ed IT leaders" and integrates with Canvas, Blackboard, Moodle, Brightspace, Banner, PeopleSoft, Workday and Colleague. No K-12 district, corporate-training or commercial buyer is named anywhere; their /customers page 404s and /solutions names no institutions, so the homepage is the only place the customer list appears. One note on our record: the category "IT & Administration" is defensible but loose — this is specifically higher-ed LMS migration and edtech data extraction, not general-purpose government IT, and a buyer at a city or county would find nothing here.

name: Mango Languages
buyer: Public libraries first — they are the headline segment and the named customers are library systems — with K-12 schools, higher education, government and military, businesses, homeschoolers and individual consumer subscribers all sold as separate packages.
note: The homepage splits the whole business into seven named segments: Libraries, K-12, Higher Ed, Business, Government, Homeschool and individual/family subscriptions. The libraries page carries the SLED evidence with real names — Cuyahoga County Public Library, Hawaii State Public Library System, Salt Lake County Library, Maryland State Library, Lexington Public Library, Pikes Peak Library District, East Baton Rouge Parish Library, Calabasas Library — and frames it as "From single branches to statewide systems." So the public-sector side is deep and specifically state-and-local, not federal window dressing. sells_outside_government is "yes" on strength of the Business segment ("equip teams for cross-cultural work") and the direct-to-consumer Individual and Family plans, which are plainly non-government buyers. Their /government page is the weakest of the set: it talks about "military and government personnel" and "civilian agencies and public-sector teams" but names no agency and leans federal/military, which is not SLED — the state and local money here clearly comes through the library and school channels instead. Our "Libraries" category is the right primary read.

name: Motorola Solutions
buyer: Law enforcement, fire and EMS agencies and corrections departments first, alongside K-12 and higher education, plus a large commercial book covering manufacturing, mining, retail, hospitality, oil and gas, utilities, transportation and logistics, healthcare and stadiums, and separately U.S. federal government and the military.
note: The homepage industry menu lists public-safety and public-sector verticals (Law Enforcement, Fire & EMS, Corrections, Education) side by side with plainly commercial ones (Manufacturing, Mining, Retail, Hospitality, Oil & Gas, Stadiums, Transportation & Logistics), and separately U.S. Federal Government and Military. Our 'Police' category is well supported by their own site, but it captures only part of the business: this is a dual public-safety/enterprise vendor, not a police-only one.

name: Palantir Technologies
buyer: Mostly large commercial enterprises by named example: Wendy's, Citi Wealth, Heineken USA, Panasonic Energy, General Mills, Lowe's, United Airlines, Airbus, Kinder Morgan, Swiss Re, Sompo, Lennar, Eaton, Archer Aviation, HCA Healthcare, Cleveland Clinic and Tampa General Hospital, with a public-sector side aimed at federal defense, intelligence and health, plus the World Food Programme.
note: Their own words: platforms are 'used throughout the public, private, and non-profit sectors.' Every customer quoted by name on the Impact page is commercial or a private hospital system. FINDING against our 'Police' category: the offerings index on that page lists Defense, Intelligence, Federal Health, Govt Financial Management, Procurement and Veterans - federal-facing - and carries no law-enforcement or police offering at all. The only state-and-local reference I found on their site is the HHS & CDC impact study describing connectivity 'across United States federal, state, and local health departments' for COVID-19. So they do sell to government, but their site does not present them as a SLED police vendor. Their main site is JavaScript-rendered and returns near-empty text to WebFetch; I read it in a browser.

name: Verkada
buyer: A broad mix of organizations: retail, manufacturing and healthcare on the commercial side, and K-12 education, cities and counties, and law enforcement on the public side, spanning what they call small and midsize businesses up to Fortune 500 leaders.
note: The homepage vertical menu names Cities & Counties, Law Enforcement and K-12 Education alongside Retail, Manufacturing and Healthcare, so both answers are directly evidenced. They claim over 30,000 organizations as customers. Our 'Police' category is supported but narrow: law enforcement is one of six named verticals, and the company sells physical security hardware broadly rather than police-specific software. Note the /industries/ path 404s; the vertical list is on the homepage.

name: Samsara
buyer: Fleet and physical-operations organizations across construction, food and beverage, field services, transportation and logistics, and passenger transit, plus a named Public Sector segment covering K-12 schools, state and local government, and higher education.
note: The industries page carries a Public Sector entry that breaks out K-12 Schools, State and Local Government, and Higher Education by name - that is SLED explicitly, not just 'government'. It sits alongside clearly commercial verticals (Construction, Food & Beverage, Transportation & Logistics, Field Services), so this is a commercial fleet-telematics vendor with a real SLED practice, matching our Fleet & Asset Mgmt category.

name: Workday
buyer: Enterprise and midsize organizations across financial services, banking, insurance, retail, manufacturing, technology, hospitality, media, communications, transportation, life sciences and professional services, plus a public-sector book covering state and local government, special districts, higher education, healthcare and nonprofits, and U.S. federal government.
note: Their industry navigation names State & Local Government, Special Districts, Higher Education and Public Sector outright, so the SLED fit for our Finance & ERP category holds. But the same menu names Banking & Capital Markets, Insurance, Retail, Hospitality, Media & Entertainment and Technology, so government is one segment of a broad horizontal HR/finance platform, not the core market. The /en-us/industries.html path 301-redirects to the homepage; the industry list is in the homepage navigation.

name: Motive
buyer: Commercial fleet operators in trucking and logistics, construction, oil and gas, agriculture, delivery, food and beverage, waste and recycling, utilities and telecom, and field service, plus state, municipal and county agencies, school districts, transit, public works and fire/police/EMS.
note: The public-sector page is unambiguously SLED: it addresses 'state, municipal, and local agencies', breaks out public works (parks and recreation, water authority, permitting/licensing/code enforcement, waste and sanitation), mass transit and school transit, and fire/police/EMS, and names three government customers - Hickman County Sheriff's Office, City of Dodge City, and Aspen School District. The commercial side is larger: the products page lists eleven industries, most of them private fleets. Good fit for our Fleet & Asset Mgmt category. Note the industries/public-sector URL 404s; the live path is /solutions/public-sector/.

name: Harris
buyer: In their own tagline, the Public Sector, Healthcare, Utilities, Private Sector and Insurance markets globally - a holding company whose acquired software businesses are each tagged to one of those five verticals.
note: Harris is a Constellation Software roll-up, not a single product company. Their Solutions page tags each acquired business unit by vertical, and Public Sector is the single most common tag across the North American portfolio - but 'Private Sector' and 'Insurance' are two of the five categories they use, which settles sells_outside_government as yes on their own labelling. Our Finance & ERP category is reasonable for the public-sector units but does not describe the whole company; a job posted under 'Harris' could belong to a utilities, healthcare or insurance business unit with no government exposure at all. Worth flagging on the board. Their site returns 403 to WebFetch; I read it in a browser.

name: Geotab
buyer: Commercial fleets across transportation and logistics, truckload carriers, courier and last-mile delivery, rental and leasing, construction, waste and recycling, utilities, mining, oil and gas, agriculture, pharmaceutical, field services, towing and dealerships, plus state and local government, public works, student transportation, police and first responders, motorpool and smart city, and federal government.
note: The industries page has a distinct public-sector block naming State and Local Government, Public Works, Student Transportation, Winter Operations, Police & First Responders, Motorpool and Smart City - all SLED - alongside Federal Government. The commercial list is roughly twice as long. Solid fit for our Fleet & Asset Mgmt category, with government as a named but minority segment.

name: Civica
buyer: Public bodies only: local and state government councils and authorities, justice and courts, healthcare, schools, colleges and libraries, social care providers and commissioners, police, and social housing organisations.
note: This is a genuine pure-play: they call themselves a 'global GovTech champion' and every buyer named is public - over 6,000 public bodies, 1,500 councils and local authorities, 3,000 schools/colleges/libraries, 2,000 care providers. No private or commercial customer appears anywhere on the page. Two caveats for the board. First, Civica is UK-origin and the scale figures (councils, Police Scotland) are UK, not US state-and-local, so their actual US SLED footprint is smaller than the headline numbers suggest. Second, on our 'Permitting & Licensing' category: the US-facing page frames the portfolio as local and state government, justice and courts, health, education, care and housing - it does not foreground permitting or licensing, so that category label is not confirmed by the page I read. Confidence is medium only because I read the US landing page rather than a US product or customer page.

name: Career TEAM
buyer: Public workforce agencies - workforce development boards, state and county government - who contract them to operate American Job Centers and who license their Career Edge platform; employers and job seekers are the people served under those contracts rather than the paying customers.
note: Their services page describes operating 50+ American Job Centers, running WIOA Title I, TANF Choices and SNAP E&T programs, and managing over $300 million in public workforce contracts - the money comes from workforce boards, states and counties, which is squarely SLED and fits our Workforce & Labor category. They do name 'Employer & Business Services' as a service line, but that is standard WIOA-funded recruitment support provided to employers at no charge under the public contract, so I read employers as beneficiaries rather than buyers and answered sells_outside_government 'no'. If the board wants to be conservative, 'cannot tell' would also be defensible there - the site never says employers pay. Worth noting their homepage is unhelpful: it reads as generic template copy ('a high-velocity digital ecosystem architected for data-driven teams') and names no customer type at all; the substance is on /services and /about. No individual client agency is named anywhere I looked, which is why confidence is medium rather than high.

name: SAND
buyer: Government agencies and ministries plus water, energy, telecom and healthcare operators — the site says it is "trusted across government, water, energy, telecom, and healthcare" and describes its users as grid controllers, water-utility ops and ministry case workers, agency managers and policy leaders.
note: Government is named repeatedly but almost always anonymised: the smart-cities case study says only "A government agency sought to understand how large-scale traffic interventions affected air quality across their capital city urban transport network," and the water-utilities case study names no utility either. The one named customer anywhere I read is Telkomsel, Indonesia's largest telecom operator (https://www.sandtech.com/telecommunications/) — a commercial carrier, which is what makes sells_outside_government yes. Language like "ministry case workers" and "capital city" points at national governments overseas rather than US states, counties or school districts; no US SLED customer is named anywhere on the site. Our "IT & AI Platforms" category fits (the Symmetri data/AI platform), but a SLED job board should know the public-sector proof here is generic, not American state and local.

name: Ivalua
buyer: Large enterprises across 11 industries, and separately a named Public Sector practice buying procurement software — state governments, cities and national governments.
note: The Public Sector industry page carries a logo wall of genuine SLED buyers: Arizona (az.gov), Ohio (ohio.gov), State of South Carolina, Commonwealth of Virginia Department of General Services, New York City, plus British Columbia Lottery Corporation and the Government of Canada. That is state and local, not just federal. The page is thin on detail — "A Proven, Reliable Partner for the Global Public Sector" and logos, no buyer-type breakdown. The homepage makes the commercial side unambiguous (IKEA, Volkswagen, Michelin, Louis Vuitton, Whirlpool, Booking.com, Crédit Agricole, Rolls Royce, BAE Systems), so public sector is one vertical of eleven, not the business. Matches our "Procurement & Payments" category.

name: Instructure
buyer: K-12 school districts and higher education institutions first, and a smaller Business & Government segment buying Canvas for corporate and association training.
note: The homepage splits the company three ways — K-12, Higher Education, Business & Government — and names public buyers directly: Hamilton County Schools (Chattanooga TN), Fairfield County Schools, Passaic County Technical Vocational Schools, University of Cincinnati, Seminole State College of Florida, University of Wyoming with five community colleges. Overwhelmingly a SLED company. sells_outside_government is yes only because of the /business page, which names PGA of America, General Assembly, USA Swimming, Kinesio University and Compass Partners in Learning alongside LA County Department of Public Health — associations, a for-profit bootcamp and nonprofits, i.e. genuinely non-public buyers. Our "IT & Administration" category understates it; this is an education (LMS) company.

name: Neara
buyer: Electric utilities and grid operators — the site's own line is "Utilities on four continents run their networks on Neara, from ambitious regional co-ops to national grid operators."
note: This is a deliberate "unclear" under house rule 1. The words government, public, municipal, state, council and agency never appear on the site describing customers — only "utilities", "co-ops" and "network operators". Electric co-ops are member-owned, not public bodies. The named US customers are all investor-owned utilities (CenterPoint Energy, Xcel Energy, Oncor, Portland General Electric), which is what makes sells_outside_government a clear yes. Several overseas names on the customer wall are state-owned in reality (ESB Networks in Ireland, HEDNO in Greece, and the Australian networks), but the site never says so, and I am not letting outside knowledge stand in for evidence. For a US state-and-local board the practical read is: no municipal/public-power utility, no state agency, no public authority is named anywhere on neara.com. Our "Grid & Energy" category is right; the SLED fit is not established by their site.

name: Emburse
buyer: Mid-to-large commercial enterprises across finance, legal, manufacturing, tech and professional services, plus a named public sector practice covering state governments and municipalities, and higher education.
note: The homepage alone would have read as purely commercial — every logo and case study there is Toyota, General Motors, Microsoft, Databricks, Garmin, General Mills, Slalom, Duane Morris LLP — and would have produced a wrong "unclear". The /industries page is where the public sector shows up: a Public Sector vertical described as covering "federal departments, agencies, contractors, state governments, municipalities," and a separate Higher Education vertical pitched on "grants, cost centers, encumbrances, travel, and study abroad expenses," which is unmistakably university back-office work. So genuine SLED, but as two verticals among fifteen. No named government or university customer appears — the public-sector claim is descriptive, not evidenced by a logo. Matches our "Procurement & Payments" category.

name: Aladtec (TCP Software)
buyer: For Aladtec itself: 24/7 public safety agencies — fire departments, EMS, law enforcement and corrections. For the parent, TCP Software, also private employers in healthcare, retail, hospitality, manufacturing and construction.
note: Two things worth flagging. First, the website on our record is stale: aladtec.com now 308-redirects to https://tcpsoftware.com/products/aladtec/ — Aladtec is a product line inside TCP Software, not a standalone site. Second, the answer depends on how you scope the company. The Aladtec product page is public-safety only ("public safety scheduling software built for 24/7 agencies") and names Gloucester County EMS, Manassas Park Fire and Rescue and the Minnesota Department of Corrections — all public, no commercial buyer at all. But TCP Software's industries page sells the same workforce-management platform to Healthcare, Retail, Hospitality, Manufacturing, Construction, Business Services and Small Business alongside Government, Public Safety, K-12 Education and Higher Education, with Marriott and Google cited as customers. I answered sells_outside_government yes for the parent; if the board means the Aladtec product narrowly, that answer would be no. Our "EMS" category is right for the product but too narrow for the vendor — Aladtec is fire/EMS/police/corrections scheduling.

name: Brinc
buyer: Public safety agencies only — police departments, sheriffs, state police, fire departments and 911/search-and-rescue agencies.
note: About as clean a SLED-only profile as this list gets. The site claims deployment "by Over 900 Public Safety Agencies in all 50 States" and names Las Vegas Metro PD, Kansas City PD, Fort Wayne PD (IN), Beverly Hills PD, Atlanta PD, Connecticut State Police, Chula Vista PD and NYPD. The pitch is literally "Put a 911 Response Drone on Every Police and Fire Station Roof" (drone-as-first-responder). No private security, no corporate, no military buyer named anywhere I read. Our "Police" category is correct, though fire and search-and-rescue are equally prominent.

name: AMCS Group
buyer: Private waste, recycling, transport and resources companies first — Recology, SUEZ Recycling and Recovery UK, Peninsula Sanitary Service, Rema — and separately municipalities buying municipal-services software.
note: The municipal-waste page is explicit about the public buyer: "A connected solution for modern municipalities. Helping to automate, optimize, and unite municipal services for safer, smarter service delivery," covering waste collection, street cleaning, winter maintenance and park upkeep — that is a city public works department. But no municipality is named; every named customer on the site is a private hauler or recycler (Recology, SUEZ, PSSI, Rema, Unicon, nemlig.com), and there are separate industry pages for Commercial & Industrial, Metal Recycling, Transport and Utilities. So the honest picture for the board is: a commercial waste-software vendor with a real municipal product line, not a government-first vendor. Our "Waste & Recycling" category is right.

name: DroneShield
buyer: Its own words: "Our capabilities are used to protect Military, Government, Law Enforcement, Critical Infrastructure, Commercial and VIPs."
note: Flagging this one for the board's purposes: the weight of the site is military and national/federal security, not state and local. The six sector pages are Military, Critical Infrastructure, Public Safety, Border Security, Aviation Facilities and Correctional Facilities — of those, only Public Safety (law enforcement), Correctional Facilities and arguably Aviation Facilities (airport authorities) are SLED. Border security is federal. "Commercial and VIPs" is named outright on the homepage, and the footer navigation lists Corporations, Events & Stadiums, Executive Protection, Maritime Security and Oil, Gas & Mining, which is why sells_outside_government is yes — I could not load those individual sector pages (/sectors/corporations 301s back to /sectors, /sectors/critical-infrastructure 404s), so the commercial detail rests on the homepage sentence and the footer, hence medium not high. No customer is named anywhere on the site. Our "Police" category captures only one slice of a counter-drone company that is primarily defence.

name: Versaterm
buyer: Public safety agencies — police and sheriffs, fire and EMS, 911 emergency communications centers and PSAPs, crime labs, court systems, and schools working with school resource officers.
note: Its "Who We Serve" menu is six industries and all six are public: Law Enforcement, Fire & EMS, ECCs & PSAPs, Crime Labs & Forensic Units, School & Education, Court Systems. Named customers are Glendale Police, Sumner County Sheriff's Office, City of Santa Monica (cloud CAD and RMS) and Charlotte County Sheriff's Office — city and county government throughout. No private security or commercial buyer appears anywhere I read. The School & Education page (https://www.versaterm.com/industry/school-education/) is about schools partnering with law enforcement on SRO programs rather than districts buying the full suite, and even there the named customer is a sheriff's office. Our "Police" category is right, though CAD/911 dispatch and courts are as central as police records.

name: ViaPath Technologies
buyer: Correctional facilities and the government agencies that run them — the site says it has partnered with more than 2,300 correctional facilities nationwide and serves "government facilities and state agencies" — with a second revenue stream from the families and friends of incarcerated people, who pay ViaPath's own consumer brands (ConnectNetwork, GettingOut, TouchPay Direct) for calls, messaging and deposits.
note: The contracting buyer is always a corrections agency — the site names no private prison operator, no commercial market, nothing outside corrections. I answered sells_outside_government "yes" only because the site runs a whole Family & Friends section (https://www.viapath.com/friends-family/) where consumers pay ViaPath brands directly for communications and deposits, and consumers count as a non-government buyer under the house rules. If you mean procurement buyers rather than end-payers, the honest answer is "no" — every contract on this site is with a public corrections agency. The site never distinguishes county jail from state DOC from federal BOP, so the SLED share is unknowable from the site. Our "Corrections" category is exactly right.

name: Robin Radar Systems
buyer: Defence ministries, air forces and national security agencies, plus airport operators and — on the bird-radar side — wind farm developers and energy companies. The homepage names the Royal Air Force, the Royal Netherlands Air Force, the Dutch Ministry of Defence, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and Amsterdam Airport Schiphol; the wind-farm page names Equinor, Eneco, Rijkswaterstaat, NINA and Waardenburg Ecology.
note: Two findings worth your attention. First, our category "Police" is not supported by their own site: their markets menu is Defence & Counter-UAS, Security, Government Infrastructure, Civil Aviation, Military Aviation, Wind Farms and Maritime — there is no law-enforcement market page and no police customer named anywhere I read. Second, the government they sell to is national and mostly European (Dutch MoD, RAF, RNLAF) or US federal (DHS), which is not SLED. The only SLED-shaped public buyers on the site are airport authorities. The non-government side is unambiguous: Equinor and Eneco are energy companies, and Boeing and Thales appear as partners/integrators.

name: Matterhorn (Court Innovations)
buyer: Courts — municipal, district, county and state trial courts. The live court list names Pinal County Superior Court (AZ), the Delaware Justice of the Peace Court, Miami-Dade's Eleventh Judicial Circuit traffic court, Coweta County State Court (GA), a dozen Michigan district courts, Suffolk County Traffic and Parking Violations Agency (NY), Maumee and Wayne County municipal courts (OH), Hamilton County General Sessions (TN) and Farmers Branch Municipal Court (TX).
note: Heads-up on the URL in our record: https://getmatterhorn.com now 301-redirects to https://catalisgov.com/matterhorn-LP — Matterhorn has been absorbed into Catalis, which describes itself as "modernizing governments across North America." The Catalis landing page names no customers at all; the actual named court list lives on courtinnovations.com, which is where I read the answer. Every buyer named on either site is a court or a public agency, so sells_outside_government is "no". Our "Courts & Case Management" category is correct, and these are state and local courts, not federal.

name: D-Fend Solutions
buyer: Counter-drone buyers across a wide sector list the company publishes itself: Military and Special Forces, National Security and Homeland Security, Law Enforcement Agencies and First Responders, Airport Safety & Security, Border Protection, VIP Protection, Maritime Security & Safety, Critical Facilities and Infrastructure, Stadiums and Arenas, Media, Prisons, Landmarks and Govt Buildings, Local Governmental, and Enterprise.

For sells_outside_government I deliberately did NOT count their "Enterprise" sector, per the house rule that the label proves nothing. What does support "yes" is "Media" (broadcasters are private companies) and "Stadiums and Arenas," whose page frames venue management as the purchaser: "Security planning for large events already requires close coordination between federal agencies, local law enforcement, private security providers, and cyber teams." Confidence is medium because no individual customer is named anywhere on the site — every sector page is written in the abstract. Caveat on category: our "Police" tag is defensible but narrow; the site leads with military and homeland security, and law enforcement is one sector of fourteen.

name: Mark43
buyer: Public safety agencies only — "over 300 public safety agencies of all sizes, from federal to state and local, across the world." Named: California Highway Patrol, Boston Police, Seattle Police, Albuquerque Police, San Antonio Police, Richmond Police, Louisville Police, DC Metropolitan Police, Morgan-style county agencies including Fresno County Sheriff and Alameda County Sheriff, San Diego Harbor Police, Elk Grove PD, plus US Secret Service, Defense Intelligence Agency, US Capitol Police and the Department of the Interior, and Cumbria Constabulary in the UK.
note: The cleanest record in this batch. Every customer named on the site is a police department, sheriff's office, campus police, port/transit police or a federal agency — no commercial buyer appears anywhere, so sells_outside_government is "no". Worth knowing for the board that their customer list mixes federal (Secret Service, DIA, Capitol Police, Interior) in with the state and local agencies; the state/local half is large and clearly the core, so this is a genuine SLED vendor, not a federal one. Our "Police" category is right, though they also serve dispatch/911 and campus and port agencies.

name: Mueller Water Products
buyer: Water and gas utilities and the municipalities that own them, alongside industrial and commercial infrastructure owners. The company describes serving "utilities and industrial and commercial water and gas infrastructure systems," and its brand pages say Singer valve solutions are used by "governments, cities, companies and contractors," with Pratt valves sold into industrial and power generation markets and Jones products into fire protection lines.
note: Their own phrase "governments, cities, companies and contractors" settles both questions in one line: cities and governments on the public side, companies and contractors on the private side. The homepage adds "industrial and commercial" explicitly and mentions data center cooling as an application, which is plainly commercial. This is a manufacturer selling largely through distributors and contractors rather than direct to agencies, so treat it as an infrastructure supplier to the SLED water market rather than a software vendor procured by a city. Our "Water" category is right but understates them — they do gas distribution and fire protection too. Note two dead URLs on their site: /about-us and /company both return 404.

name: Knightscope
buyer: Whoever runs physical security at a site — the homepage addresses "the Chief Security Officers of the United States of America" and lists the verticals it protects as Retail, Industrial, Healthcare and Education, with imagery and copy covering parking lots, big-box stores, storage yards, hospital campuses, school entrances, residential communities, casinos and utility sites. It claims 434 clients across 42 US states but names not one of them.
note: Two problems, and you should treat this record as unfinished. First, their site is a single-page app that returned the identical homepage shell for every sub-URL I tried (/the-force, /comms, /briefing, /use-cases/who-we-serve, /use-cases/schools, /use-cases/federal) — so I could not actually read any of the pages that would answer the government question, and /clients and /industries 404. The only government evidence I could read anywhere was "Government / Federal" appearing as an option in an inquiry form's sector dropdown, which is not a claim about customers, so I set sells_to_gov to "unclear" rather than "yes". A page titled "Federal Government | Knightscope" does exist in their nav but I could not retrieve its contents, and I have not counted it. Second, and more actionable: our category "Park Assets, Forestry & Visitor Data" does not match this company at all. Knightscope makes autonomous security robots and emergency blue-light communication towers — it is a physical-security vendor. That category should be corrected. sells_outside_government is "yes" with real confidence: retail, casinos, residential communities and corporate sites are unambiguously private buyers and all appeared in readable homepage copy.

name: Flock Safety
buyer: Both halves of the market, openly. Public: police and sheriffs (Fort Worth PD, Castle Rock PD, Whitehall PD, Morgan Hill PD, Spokane County Sheriff's Office, Tulsa PD), school districts (Spring Branch ISD, Licking Heights Schools), the University of Iowa, plus corrections and parks agencies. Private: HOAs and neighborhood associations, multifamily communities, retail and grocery (Academy Sports is named), retail banking, healthcare, hospitality, logistics, manufacturing, builders and developers, property managers and places of worship.
note: Their customers page states the split itself: "5,000+ Law Enforcement Agencies," "6,000+ Communities" and "1,000+ Businesses." The HOA page makes the private buyer explicit — "Your HOA owns all footage and data" and "Law enforcement only gains access if your HOA opts in" — so the HOA, not a city, is the contracting party there. Our "Police" category captures their largest and most visible segment and is fair, but be aware roughly half their published industry pages are commercial; if the board ever filters on "government-only vendors," Flock should not be in that bucket.

name: Gridware
buyer: Electric utilities of every ownership type. The customers page states they partner with "Investor-Owned Utilities (IOU), Customer-Owned Utilities (COU), Electric Cooperatives, Municipal Utilities, and Public Utility Districts," and the case studies name PG&E, Puget Sound Energy, Xcel Energy and Brigham City Public Power.
note: This one is genuinely mixed and the site says so in a single sentence. Municipal Utilities and Public Utility Districts are public buyers and there is a named example — "Brigham City Public Power Averts Wildfire on Festival Day." But the marquee case studies are PG&E, Puget Sound Energy and Xcel Energy, which are investor-owned, i.e. private companies, and electric cooperatives are member-owned rather than public. So the public-power share of their business looks like the minority. Our "Grid & Energy" category is right. If the board is trying to surface SLED-relevant roles, the municipal-utility and PUD side is the part that qualifies.

name: CORE Business Technologies
buyer: Mostly local government — "1,000+ Government Agencies Served" across "49 U.S. States with Active Clients," reaching "28% of the U.S. Population," with the product aimed at Finance Directors, IT Directors and City Managers. Named clients are counties and cities: Grand County UT, Washington County UT, Beaver County UT, Juab County UT and the City of Davenport IA. They also publish Healthcare and Higher Education verticals.

I set sells_outside_government to "yes" on thinner evidence: their healthcare page quotes a clinical informatics specialist at Jefferson Health, a private nonprofit health system, and references "enterprise retail and ambulatory pharmacies," which are commercial. That page never states whether its hospital buyers are public or private, so the non-government read rests on the Jefferson Health mention plus retail pharmacy. Higher education counts as public under our rules either way. Our "Procurement & Payments" category fits — they are a payments and revenue-collection platform for local government.

name: StarRez
buyer: Primarily universities and colleges managing on-campus housing, alongside private purpose-built student accommodation (PBSA) operators, build-to-rent and co-living developments, boarding schools and staff-housing operators.
note: The homepage lists its markets as Higher Education, Student Property Management (PBSA), Build to Rent, Boarding Schools, Co-Living, Staff Housing and Conference & Events, and names public universities (Montana State, University of Oregon, University of Oklahoma, Oklahoma State) next to Abodus, a private UK student-accommodation operator. Our category of 'IT & Administration' is fair but understates how specifically this is student-housing software.

name: InvoiceCloud
buyer: Local governments, county tax offices and public utilities/water districts taking resident bill payments, plus insurance carriers collecting premiums and paying claims.

name: Everbridge
buyer: State and local governments and public safety agencies sending resident alerts, universities, and hospitals, alongside a large commercial book: banks, manufacturers, retailers, insurers and global corporations managing employee safety.

It equally names Goldman Sachs, Royal Bank of Canada, Siemens, Sony PlayStation and Diebold Nixdorf, so the commercial market is named outright, not inferred from a segment label. Clean fit for our 'Emergency Mgmt' category.

name: The Weather Company
buyer: Airlines and their dispatch and ground-operations teams, broadcast and digital media newsrooms, advertisers and brands, insurers and energy companies, government and defense agencies, plus consumers through The Weather Channel, Weather Underground and Storm Radar apps.

Commercial breadth is beyond doubt (NASCAR, CAA Club Group, advertising, consumer apps). Confidence is medium only because sells_to_gov rests on a federal/defense page and the state-and-local relevance this board cares about is not demonstrated on their site.

name: VertiGIS
buyer: Local governments, public safety and transportation authorities, and public utilities, alongside private utilities, telecom network operators, oil and gas firms, engineering and construction companies, manufacturers and real-estate/facility managers.

name: ROLLER
buyer: Privately operated attractions and leisure venues - trampoline parks, family entertainment centres, water parks, escape rooms, climbing gyms, play centres and theme parks.

name: Dataminr
buyer: Corporate security, cyber and risk teams at large enterprises (two-thirds of the Fortune 50), financial services and insurance firms, newsrooms, and government agencies including US federal and defense customers.

name: Pointr
buyer: Large private enterprises for indoor mapping and wayfinding — retailers, workplaces and pharma — alongside airport operators and hospital systems.
note: The commercial market is unambiguous and is clearly the bulk of the business: The Home Depot (2,300 stores), Microsoft, Cisco, Nike, KPMG, EY, PwC, Siemens, Honeywell, Sanofi, and sectors named as Workplace, Events, Retail, Hospitality. Worth a human deciding whether public power utilities belong on this board at all.

name: Acentra Health
buyer: State health and Medicaid agencies, plus the federal Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services.
note: Cleanest case in this batch. Our 'Benefits & Medicaid Systems' category is accurate.

name: GoGuardian
buyer: K-12 school districts — district administrators, IT staff and teachers.
note: The site is single-market and says so: 'The #1 choice for K-12 web filtering on any OS', 'Supporting 50% of US K-12 students', '2M+ educators'. name: CaseGuard
buyer: Police departments, sheriffs' offices and city and county government for video redaction, and equally a broad commercial market including casinos, retailers, insurers, banks and law firms.

buyer: Retailers, primarily — the platform is sold to retail chains, with law enforcement agencies presented as a second audience that collaborates on the same network.
note: This one needs a human call and I want to be plain about why. name: Wastequip
buyer: Waste hauling companies and municipalities, plus industrial, commercial and institutional customers across North America.

Caveat for the board: this is a manufacturer of dumpsters, compactors and roll-off containers selling largely through distribution, and it names no individual customer anywhere on the site — no case studies, no customer logos, no markets pages. So the categories are their own words but there is no named-account evidence behind either answer. Our 'Waste & Recycling' category fits.

name: Frontline Wildfire Defense
buyer: Homeowners, first and foremost, plus production homebuilders, architects and contractors, wineries and vineyards, summer camps and commercial property owners.

name: Hello Heart
buyer: Self-insured employers first, plus health plans, public-sector employers and labor unions — sold as a benefit to a workforce, not to a government program.
note: The site has a dedicated /for-businesses/public-sector page alongside /employers, /health-plans and /labor-unions. name: Sentinel Offender Services
buyer: County sheriffs, district attorneys, courts and community-supervision agencies that need electronic monitoring and GPS tracking of offenders.
note: Named customers in the homepage testimonials are Riverside County Sheriff's Department (CA), Canyon County Sheriff's Office (ID), and a chief attorney from the Wichita, Kansas District Attorney's office; the site claims use in 48 states.
