name: Zenner USA
buyer: Water utilities, sold largely through a distributor network; the hydrant-meter page names municipalities and businesses as the users being billed for.
note: This site names no customer anywhere — no case studies, no logos, no customers page; the contact structure is distributors by state and regional sales managers, so they sell through channel. The only buyer language I could find on their own pages: the hydrant-meter page says the meters let 'municipalities and businesses' track and bill water usage from hydrants; the About page refers to 'the utilities we serve' and to water-utility tradeshows; the AMR/AMI page says the system is 'designed from the ground up for utility and industrial applications.' That is enough for yes on both questions but not for high confidence, and I would not claim any specific public customer. /about-us, /company and /water-meters all 404 — the live paths are /about and /products. Our 'Water' category is right.

name: Stellic
buyer: Colleges and universities — registrars, provosts, advisors and CIOs at large public universities, community colleges, R1 research institutions and small private colleges.
note: Customer logos and success stories are entirely higher education: public institutions include Florida State, University of Virginia, The Ohio State University, Indiana University, University of Nebraska, University of Utah, Santa Monica College and Johnson County Community College; private ones include Carnegie Mellon, Cornell, Duke, Johns Hopkins, Columbia, Wesleyan, Quinnipiac, TCU, Case Western and Colorado College. Under the house rule that colleges and universities are public buyers whether public or private, that makes sells_outside_government a no. Some customers are foreign (UNSW Sydney, University of Newcastle Australia, Qatar University), which is outside SLED geographically but still public. One correction to our record: 'IT & Administration' undersells it — this is higher-ed student-success, degree-audit and academic-planning software, and the buyer is the registrar/provost office, so a Higher Ed or Student Success category would fit better.

name: Routeware
buyer: Two distinct markets it addresses separately on its own site: city and county waste operations, and private waste haulers.
note: The site is split into 'For Governments' (routeware.com/for-governments/) and 'For Haulers' (routeware.com/for-waste-haulers/), and claims 1,500 customers worldwide. Named public buyers: City of Atlanta, City of Denver, City of Austin, University of Michigan, and Falkirk Council in the UK. Named private buyers: Waste Pro and Casella Waste Systems, both commercial haulers. So this is unambiguously a both-sides vendor. Minor note: www.routeware.com 301-redirects to the bare http://routeware.com/, which is where I read this. Our 'Waste & Recycling' category is correct.

name: BS&A Software
buyer: Local governments only — cities, townships, towns and counties buying financial management, HR, utility billing, community development and assessing/property tax software.
note: The homepage headline is ERP software designed for local government and claims 2,100+ organizations. The case studies page confirms it with named customers and nothing else: Big Rapids MI, Northville Township MI, New Buffalo MI, Lowell AR, North Little Rock AR, Streetsboro OH, Brainerd MN, Cape Canaveral FL, Cooper City FL, Gulf Breeze FL, Dahlonega GA, Woodstock GA, Easley SC, Angola IN, Chester NH, Greenfield WI, Overland MO and Cole County MO. Every one is a municipal or county government; no school district and no commercial customer appears. Heavy Michigan concentration, which matches their own 'a majority of Michigan municipalities' claim. Our 'Finance & ERP' category is right.

name: ICC Innovation
buyer: Local jurisdictions — building departments, towns, boroughs and counties buying codification, ePermitting, electronic plan review and code-enforcement tools.
note: The Innovation page itself is a portfolio index rather than a product page — it points at Digital Codes Premium, General Code (eCode360, eCode ALP, MapLink/ZoningHub), American Legal Publishing, and ICC Community Development Solutions (Municity, DigEplan, Laserfiche), plus ICC Online Learning and PRONTO testing. Its only buyer language is aimed at jurisdictions: enabling 'employees and citizens' to conduct business from anywhere, and providing 'your constituents' with options that help your community grow. Named public customers come from the Municity product page on ICC's own icc-cds.com: Southeast Ohio Building Department, Borough of Emmaus PA, Town of Dover NY, Town of Glenville, and the Government of the US Virgin Islands. I set sells_outside_government to 'cannot tell' deliberately: ICC's Digital Codes Premium and professional development are widely bought by architects, engineers and contractors too, but codes.iccsafe.org returned HTTP 403 so I could not confirm that on their own site, and no ICC page I could read names a private buyer. One caveat for the board: 'ICC Innovation' is a product-suite landing page inside the International Code Council's site, not a standalone company, and our 'Suppliers & Services' category does not describe it — this is govtech software (permitting, plan review, codification).

name: Rain Bird
buyer: Rain Bird sells irrigation equipment through six named customer segments on its own navigation - homeowners, landscape contractors, golf courses, agriculture/farms, public agencies, and commercial/sports-turf projects - so public agencies are one division of a much broader consumer and commercial business.
note: The homepage nav lists 'Public Agency' as a first-class customer segment alongside Homeowners, Landscape Professionals, Golf Course Irrigation and Agriculture, and rainbird.com/agency is a dedicated agency portal (training, rewards, water-efficiency, sports turf, and California's MWELO ordinance). That page names no individual city, parks department, school or water district as a customer, which is why confidence is medium rather than high - the segment is clearly real, the named references are not. Outside government is unambiguous: homeowners, golf courses and farms are not public buyers. Worth knowing for the board: Rain Bird is a manufacturer with a public-agency division, not a govtech vendor, so SLED is a minority of its business.

name: ParkHub
buyer: ParkHub no longer exists under that name - parkhub.com 301-redirects to justpark.com/business, and the company's own rebrand post says the combined business serves stadiums and entertainment venues, airports, universities, parking operators, commercial real estate, hospitality and UK local authorities.
note: IMPORTANT DATA ISSUE: https://parkhub.com and https://www.parkhub.com both return HTTP 301 to https://www.justpark.com/business/. ParkHub merged with UK-based JustPark and rebranded as JustPark in April 2025, so the board's company name and URL are both stale. Reading the successor's own site: the rebrand post names Rose Bowl (owned by the City of Pasadena), Las Vegas Convention Center (Las Vegas Convention and Visitors Authority, a public authority), Reno Tahoe International Airport (an airport authority) and US university campus parking - all public buyers - which is what supports sells_to_gov yes. It also names Mercedes-Benz Stadium and lists Parking Operators, Commercial Real Estate and Hospitality as segments, and the UK business page names Hilton, Sainsbury's and ASDA, so it plainly sells outside government too. The UK business page does list a 'Local Authorities & Public Sector' sector (/uk/business/sectors/local-authority), but that is the UK side. Confidence is medium only because no page under the ParkHub name survives to verify against.

name: Recidiviz
buyer: Recidiviz is a nonprofit that partners with state criminal justice agencies - its homepage names the Michigan, Colorado, North Dakota and Maine departments of corrections and claims experience across 20 states.
note: Every buyer named on the site is a state department of corrections; the site describes itself as a nonprofit that 'partners with criminal justice agencies,' so 'sells' is a loose fit but the buyer relationship is unambiguous and entirely state government. No commercial, private-prison or vendor customer appears anywhere on the homepage. Our 'Corrections' category is accurate. The platform is pitched as working 'alongside or in place of your current software,' i.e. it sits next to incumbent DOC case management systems.

name: Overstory
buyer: Overstory sells vegetation and wildfire-risk intelligence to electric utilities - its named customers are investor-owned utilities (PG&E, AEP, Eversource, ComEd, Portland General, Mississippi Power, Oklahoma Gas & Electric) and rural electric cooperatives (Holy Cross Energy, Sho-Me Power, Powder River, Central Virginia Electric, Inland Power), not government agencies.
note: This one does not fit the board's premise well. Every US customer named on the homepage, case studies and /wildfire page is an investor-owned utility or a member-owned electric cooperative - both private entities, not public buyers. The only publicly-owned utilities named are foreign: BC Hydro (British Columbia crown corporation), Hydro Ottawa (owned by the City of Ottawa), Copel (Brazilian state-controlled) and Red Electrica (Spain). No US state, county, city, fire agency or land-management agency appears anywhere I read, so sells_to_gov is 'unclear' for SLED purposes rather than 'no' - the foreign public utilities are real public buyers, just not US state-and-local. Our 'Fire' category is defensible in subject matter (wildfire risk, /wildfire page) but misleading in buyer: the wildfire product is sold to utility vegetation-management teams, not fire departments.

name: Clariti
buyer: Clariti sells permitting, licensing and land-management software exclusively to local governments, naming the City of Los Angeles, City of Phoenix, Orange County CA, Dona Ana County NM, City of Albany NY, City and County of Honolulu, City of Santa Clarita and City of Tampa.
note: Clean SLED-only vendor. The site tiers its products explicitly by government size - Enterprise for 'large local governments,' Launch for 'small to mid-sized local governments,' CivCheck for 'governments of all sizes' - which is a good example of house rule 2: the word 'Enterprise' here means a big city, not a commercial market. No private-sector buyer is named anywhere. Our 'Permitting & Licensing' category matches the site exactly.

name: Concourse Tech
buyer: Concourse Tech sells to public institutions only - its own words are 'State agencies, cities and counties, school districts, colleges and universities, special districts,' and it claims more than 100 public sector organizations 'from rural towns to enormous state agencies.'
note: The case studies confirm it: City of Owosso MI, Rides Mass Transit District IL, Houston-Galveston Area Council, State of Oklahoma OMES, a regional transit authority, a county parks department, an urban school district, a community college, a state treasury, a state judiciary and a state water resources board. Not one private business appears. Note the product footprint is far wider than our 'Procurement & Payments' category - the site lists twelve solution areas including permitting, legislative/public meetings, utility billing, courts and public safety, parks and recreation, grants, and asset management. Most case studies anonymize the customer ('a West Coast city,' 'a state treasury department'), so the named-logo evidence is thinner than the volume of case studies suggests.

name: InVita Healthcare Technologies
buyer: InVita sells mainly to healthcare organizations - hospitals and health systems, blood and plasma centers, organ/eye/tissue donation organizations, ambulatory surgery centers and pharmaceutical companies - with one forensic product line aimed at 'crime labs and CODIS labs' and sexual assault kit tracking programs.
note: Our 'Police' category is a stretch and should probably be revisited. Three of InVita's four solution lines are healthcare (blood management, donation/transplant, tissue/implant); only the STACS forensic DNA line touches public safety, and even there the stated buyer is the crime lab and CODIS lab, not a police department - the site never uses the words 'police,' 'law enforcement,' 'medical examiner' or 'coroner' on the pages I read. Government is inferable because US CODIS labs and statewide sexual assault kit tracking programs are state/local agencies, but InVita does not say so itself, hence medium confidence on sells_to_gov. Outside government is beyond doubt: named customers include Mayo Clinic, Merck, New York Blood Center, OneBlood, ProMedica, Atlantic Health System, Versiti and Donor Network of Arizona. Note /solutions/dna-forensic-sample-management/ 404s; the working path is under /who-we-serve/.

name: Nutanix
buyer: Nutanix sells cloud/HCI infrastructure across ten named industries - financial services, retail, manufacturing, automotive, healthcare, media, pharma, legal, service providers and government and education - with a dedicated state-and-local page naming County of San Mateo, Harris County TX, City of Cape Coral, City of Westfield MA, California Office of Emergency Services and Bay Area Rapid Transit.
note: Both answers are firmly documented on their own pages. The state-and-local page names six SLED customers including a transit authority (BART) and a state emergency-management agency, and the site splits Government and Education into Federal, State and Local, and Education sub-pages. Equally clearly commercial: Home Depot, Caterpillar, Vodafone, Edward Jones, Westgate Resorts and London Gatwick Airport appear on the homepage, and it claims 32,000+ companies. SLED is one vertical inside a large global enterprise vendor, not the business - relevant if the board wants to flag how much of a company's hiring is actually public-sector.

name: FLASH
buyer: FLASH sells parking and mobility technology to seven named verticals - Municipalities, Airport, Higher Education, Healthcare, Venues & Events, Commercial Real Estate (REITs) and New Build/Design - so public and private buyers sit side by side on the same page.
note: Public evidence is specific, not just a vertical label: Denver International Airport ('144 lanes in only 22 days'), Oakland California (446 EV chargers funded by a California Energy Commission grant), and more than 30 Philadelphia locations launching Express Pay. Commercial evidence is equally plain - Commercial Real Estate/REITs, hospitality valet operations, and a Waze integration covering 30K locations. Our 'Parking & Ground Transport' category matches. Note this is the same market as the ParkHub/JustPark record, so the two entries overlap.

name: Emergency Reporting
buyer: Emergency Reporting is now part of ESO and its own site only says it serves 'first responders' across 'the entire health and public safety spectrum,' while ESO's site organizes its buyers into four segments - Fire, EMS, Hospital and Government - and names South Snohomish County Fire Rescue on the fire page.
note: DATA ISSUE: emergencyreporting.com is now a transition page - no products, no customers, no solutions nav - that states Emergency Reporting is part of ESO and directs visitors to ESO.com and an ESO demo form. The board should probably fold this record into ESO or mark it acquired. Sells_to_gov is yes on the strength of ESO's Fire and Government segments plus the one named fire customer, South Snohomish County Fire Rescue, a public regional fire authority. Sells_outside_government is 'cannot tell' deliberately: Emergency Reporting's own pages name no buyer at all, and the only hospital named on ESO's site is Children's Hospital Colorado, a private nonprofit - so the parent does appear to sell beyond government, but the fire/EMS records product this record is about serves public fire and EMS agencies. A human should decide whether to score the parent or the product.

name: Embross
buyer: Airlines and airport/port authorities buy Embross self-service kiosks, bag-drop and biometric boarding hardware — the homepage names Delta Air Lines, Port of Oakland, Calgary Airport, Billy Bishop Airport, Aeroport Marseille Provence and the Turks and Caicos Islands Airports Authority.
note: Split buyer. Public side is real but is airport and port authorities (Port of Oakland, Turks and Caicos Islands Airports Authority) rather than states, counties or school districts; commercial side is airlines, with Delta Air Lines called out for 'the first biometric terminal in the U.S.' The case-studies index (https://www.embross.com/case-studies/) is mostly non-US airports (Nuremberg, Deauville-Normandie, Greenland, Ivory Coast, La Reunion, Indian airports), so US SLED exposure looks narrow — essentially airport and port authorities. Our 'Terminal & Passenger Experience' category is accurate.

name: Tantalus Systems
buyer: Community-scale electric utilities — the homepage says it serves 'public power and electric cooperative utilities' and claims more than 320 utility partners; case studies name Farmersville Utilities & Public Works, Estes Park Light and Power, BrightRidge, Highland (IL), BEA, La Plata Electric Association and Appalachian Electric Coop.
note: Public power utilities are city- or district-owned, so this is squarely a local-government buyer (Farmersville Utilities & Public Works, Estes Park Light and Power are city utilities). The 'yes' on selling outside government is a technicality worth reading carefully: the other half of the named base is electric cooperatives (La Plata Electric Association, Appalachian Electric Coop, Tri-County), which are member-owned private nonprofits, not public authorities. There is no commercial or investor-owned market named — the site explicitly positions against large IOUs. If the board treats co-ops as public-adjacent, this is effectively a pure public-power vendor.

name: OCLC
buyer: Libraries of every type, as members rather than ordinary customers — the site's own navigation splits them into public, academic, school, research, special libraries and groups/consortia.
note: sells_to_gov is not in doubt: public libraries, K-12 school libraries and public universities are named buyer categories with their own landing pages. The 'yes' on outside-government is marginal and I want to flag it rather than let it stand plainly. The only non-public buyers I could find named anywhere are on the special-libraries page (https://www.oclc.org/en/special.html): The Huntington Library, described there as a private research library, and the Victoria and Albert Museum's National Art Library. Everything else on that page is also public (CSIC and CSIRO are national research councils; the Harry Ransom Center is at UT Austin). So there is no commercial market here at all — private nonprofit research libraries and museums are the entire exception. If the board's rule counts 'libraries' as public regardless of ownership, this should read 'no'. The homepage names no specific customer; it describes itself as 'a member-driven library organization'.

name: KloudGin
buyer: Municipalities and public-sector utility operators — the public-sector page promises 'work and asset management solutions for municipalities and the public sector' and the only named customer anywhere on the site is the City of Pasadena, for water and electric asset and construction work management.
note: Strong public-sector evidence, thin evidence either way on a commercial market. KloudGin runs vertical pages for water/wastewater, gas, electric, telecom and refuse, and in the US gas and electric verticals would normally mean investor-owned utilities — but the site never names one. The gas page says only 'best in class work and asset management solutions for gas utilities' with no customer. The telecom and refuse pages sit under the municipal/public-sector umbrella, not as commercial telco offerings. The one private company named, Black & Veatch, is announced as a delivery partner, not a customer. So: certainly sells to local government, and I cannot tell from their own site whether they also sell to private utilities. Our 'Fleet & Asset Mgmt' category is roughly right but understates it — this is field service plus enterprise asset plus construction work management.

name: Ease Health
buyer: Behavioral health treatment organizations — addiction treatment centers, MAT clinics, IOP/PHP programs, residential facilities, outpatient practices and community mental health centers; the homepage names Youth Health Associates, Sandia Crest, Christian Counseling Associates, Sophros, Canopy Pines, Grand Union Holistic, American School for the Deaf and MONARCH, Inc.
note: This one does not look like a SLED vendor on its own evidence, and I think that is a finding worth surfacing. The site is a CRM/EHR/RCM platform sold to provider organizations; the solutions page (https://easehealth.com/solutions) lists only facility types, and the three case studies (https://easehealth.com/case-studies) are Christian Counseling Associates, Treatment Trends and NOW Counseling — all private or nonprofit providers. No county behavioral health department, state agency or public health system appears anywhere I looked. 'Community Mental Health Centers' is the closest thing, and some CMHCs are county-run, but the site never says so. American School for the Deaf and MONARCH, Inc. are private nonprofits, not public agencies. Our 'Behavioral Health' category is correct as a subject matter, but the buyer is private-sector, so I set sells_to_gov to unclear rather than yes.

name: Aurelian
buyer: 911 centers — PSAPs and emergency communications centers, plus sheriff's offices; the customers page names Volusia Sheriff's Office, Snohomish County 911, Kalamazoo County, Hamilton County 911, Cowlitz 911, Summit ECC, Akron Safety Communications, PenCom, MACC 911, MACECOM and South Summit Dispatch.
note: As pure a local-government buyer as this list gets — every named customer is a county 911 center, a sheriff's office or a municipal dispatch agency, and the products (AVA for non-emergency call handling, CORA for live call guidance) have no non-government use case on the site. Two housekeeping notes for the board. First, the URL we carry is stale: https://www.aurelian.io 308-redirects to https://www.aurelian.com/, so the record should be updated. Second, our category says 'EMS' — the site is about PSAP/911 dispatch generally, covering law enforcement, fire and EMS calls, so '911 / Emergency Communications' would describe it better.

name: RecDesk
buyer: Recreation organizations — municipal parks and recreation departments first, alongside aquatic centers, community centers, schools and universities, homeowners associations and nonprofits.
note: Parks and rec departments are the lead segment on the homepage and have their own page (/parks-and-recreation/), so the local-government buyer is clear. The outside-government answer rests on a dedicated HOA page (https://www.recdesk.com/hoa/), which says 'Homeowners Associations across the country rely on RecDesk' for managing pools, tennis courts, cabanas and resident memberships — an HOA is a private community association, not a public body — plus a named nonprofit segment. Customer names on the site are thin: testimonials are first-name only with town references (Goffstown, Somerton), and there is no case-study library. Our 'Recreation Management' category is accurate.

name: AiDash
buyer: Electric and gas utilities buying satellite-based vegetation management, asset inspection and wildfire/storm risk software; the customer-stories page names Entergy, Xcel Energy, National Grid, Alabama Power, PNM, SWEPCO, El Paso Electric, Avista, Nova Scotia Power alongside Omaha Public Power District, Klickitat PUD, Trinity PUD and several rural co-ops.
note: Genuinely mixed, and the commercial half is the larger half. The public buyers are real SLED entities — Omaha Public Power District is a political subdivision of Nebraska, and Klickitat and Trinity PUDs are public utility districts, which are special districts. But most named logos are investor-owned utilities (Entergy, Xcel, National Grid, Alabama Power, Avista), which are private companies. The homepage also lists mining and transportation as served industries, which pushes further commercial. Our 'Grid & Energy' category fits; a board reader should know that a job here is more likely to be an IOU account than a municipal one.

name: SOVRA
buyer: Two sides of the same marketplace: public procurement teams — states, counties, cities, school districts and universities — and, on paid subscriptions, the private suppliers bidding into them.
note: The strongest SLED record in this batch. The homepage names more than twenty public buyers including the states of Oregon, New Jersey, Nevada, Massachusetts and Illinois, Fulton County, Pima County, Bexar County, Dutchess County, the cities of Knoxville, Boulder, Pensacola and Newburgh, Albany County Airport Authority, Dearborn Public Schools, Georgetown ISD, Texas A&M San Antonio, Colorado State, Oakland University and Seminole State College. The outside-government 'yes' is not a commercial pivot — it is the supplier side of the same network: https://www.sovra.com/pricing-suppliers/ sells private vendors Bidnet Direct subscriptions at $100 to $330 a month and MERX for Canadian tenders, so companies pay to find public bids. Note that a meaningful share of named buyers are Canadian (City of Ottawa, Newfoundland & Labrador, MERX), so not every role will be US SLED. Our 'Procurement & Payments' category is correct.

name: Starbridge
buyer: Go-to-market teams at private companies that sell into government and education — sales leaders, SDR/BDR and account-executive teams; named customers are Fortinet, Airtable, Instructure, Clever, MagicSchool, Aramark, Bobcat, Ramp, Zencity, Mark43, McGraw Hill, Panorama Education, ClearGov, SimpliGov and similar vendors.
note: This contradicts our record and the board should look at it. We have Starbridge filed under 'Procurement & Payments', which reads as software an agency buys. It is the opposite: a sales-intelligence and RFP-discovery platform sold to the vendors chasing public contracts. The site says it serves '500+ GTM teams selling to government agencies, K-12, and higher education', and every named customer on the testimonials page is a private company — several of them other govtech vendors (Mark43, Zencity, ClearGov, SimpliGov, GovWell, Kaizen Labs). Agencies are the subject of Starbridge's data, not its buyers; I found no government agency shown as a paying customer. I set sells_to_gov to 'no' rather than 'unclear' because the site is explicit and consistent about who pays. It is still govtech-adjacent, and jobs there are public-sector-facing sales roles, so the board may want to keep it — but not as a vendor that sells to SLED.

name: Monday.com
buyer: Commercial enterprises and SMBs first — Coca-Cola, McDonald's, Canva, Universal Music Group, Lionsgate, Carrefour — with a dedicated public-sector vertical that claims 800+ state and local government agency clients.
note: Horizontal work-management platform, not a govtech company. The homepage lists Government alongside Retail/CPG, Technology, Manufacturing, Advertising and Media as industries, and names only commercial logos. The public-sector page claims '800+ state and local government agency clients' and 'Trusted by government organizations across the nation', but names exactly one public customer: a testimonial from the Sr. Director of Enterprise PMO at San Diego County Office of Education. It also cites NASCIO and NACo as partnerships, not customers. So SLED is real but is one vertical of a mostly commercial business — our 'IT & AI Platforms' category is fair, but a job seeker should not expect a government-focused employer.

name: Outsight SA
buyer: Operators of large physical sites — airports first (Dallas Fort Worth, Rome Fiumicino/Aeroporti di Roma, Groupe ADP), plus a named US city (City of Bellevue, smart intersections), alongside hospitals, retail, quick-service restaurants, manufacturing and distribution centers.
note: WebFetch and curl both got a Cloudflare 403 on this domain; I read the homepage through a real browser instead, so the evidence is first-hand. Industry list on the homepage is explicitly split into Smart Places (Hospitals, Retail, Tourism & Stadiums, Quick Service Restaurants), Transportation Hubs (Airports, Railway Stations, Ports & Seaways, Public Transport), Industrial & Logistics (Manufacturing, Distribution Centers, Energy) and Government (Smart Cities, Highways & Roads, Multi-Modal Transportation, Parking Monitoring, Curbside & Intersections). Public buyers are named directly: City of Bellevue on smart intersections, and DFW Airport (an airport authority) for 'the World's Largest 3D LiDAR Deployment'. Our 'Terminal & Passenger Experience' category matches the aviation half but understates a company that is equally industrial and retail, and it is a French firm whose flagship references are European airports.

name: SimpliGov
buyer: State and local government agencies only — State of California, State of New Jersey, City of San Jose, City of Cupertino, Guilford County NC, and the California Community Colleges Board of Governors.
note: Purely public-sector. Positions itself as 'The platform government programs run on'. Solutions are organized by government function on both the constituent side (vehicle & transportation, licensing & permitting, health & human services, public safety & justice) and the internal side (HR, procurement & finance, legal & compliance, IT & administration). No commercial customer, industry or use case appears anywhere on the homepage. Our 'Citizen Services' category fits, though the internal-operations half (HR, procurement) is just as prominent as citizen-facing services.

name: iWorQ Systems
buyer: Cities and counties — specifically community development and public works departments; North Ogden, UT is the one named client.
note: Local government only, and says so plainly: 'Local Government Software Solutions' and 'Management Software Built for Community Development & Public Works Departments'. Reinforced by '100% U.S. Owned & Operated' and hosting on AWS GovCloud. No private-sector buyer named anywhere. Our 'Citizen Services' category is defensible but the product is really departmental operations software for public works and community development (permits, code enforcement, asset management) rather than a resident-facing portal.

name: Authorium
buyer: Government agencies — state and local first (CalPERS is the named customer), plus federal work with the U.S. Air Force.
note: Public-sector only; no commercial buyer named. Describes itself as 'A single platform to transform documents and data into operational value and connect the flow of public funds across mission-critical government functions', and says roughly 60% of its staff have worked in government. FINDING: our category 'HR & Workforce' looks wrong. The site's named functions are procurement, contract lifecycle management, budget requests, grants management and legislative analysis — that is procurement/contracting and grants, not HR. Worth re-categorizing. Also note the federal U.S. Air Force work sits outside SLED, though CalPERS is squarely state.

name: EMS LINQ
buyer: K-12 school districts first — Culver City, Eagle County, Hernando, Mesa, Willard, St. Vrain Valley School District CO — plus state education agencies.
note: Entirely K-12 public education. Mission line on the homepage is 'Feed every kid. Pay every teacher. Use every dollar.' Buyer personas are named by district role: nutrition leaders, finance and business operations leaders, HR leaders, superintendents, technology directors. Product lines are school nutrition, K-12 ERP ('budgets, payroll, and more with tools built for the way K-12 districts actually work') and payments. No non-education buyer appears. Our 'Operations & SIS' category is close but slightly off: LINQ is nutrition + ERP + payments, not a student information system.

name: ClassLink
buyer: K-12 school systems first (Rowan-Salisbury Schools, Collierville ISD, Harwood Unified Union SD, South Heart Schools), plus colleges and community colleges (Cedar Crest College, Laramie County Community College, Dunwoody College of Technology) and statewide education agencies.
note: Education only. Homepage claims '3,000+ School Systems', '25M+ Students & Staff', '50 States', '42 Countries' and says the products are 'built for education'. Beyond K-12 the site carries a higher-ed overview naming colleges and community colleges and a statewide solution plus a StateLink product for state education agencies — all still public/institutional buyers under the SLED definition, so nothing here counts as an outside-government market. Our 'Operations & SIS' category fits loosely; the actual product is identity, single sign-on and rostering rather than a student information system.

name: PURVIS Systems
buyer: City and county fire, EMS and 911 dispatch agencies (FDNY, Boston Fire, Washington DC, Jacksonville, Naperville IL, Charleston County SC, Williamson County TX) alongside a long-running federal defense business with the U.S. Navy, NIH and Fort Detrick — and, on the defense side, private prime contractors and small businesses.
note: Two distinct businesses. The SLED half is fire station alerting and dispatch for municipal and county public-safety agencies — 'trusted advisor to FDNY for 45+ years', Charleston County covering '2 dispatch locations, and 75+ fire & EMS departments'. The defense half is federal: 'trusted partner to the U.S. Navy for over 40 years', NIH, Fort Detrick, and CMMC Level 2 certification. The only non-public buyer is on the defense page, which says PURVIS is 'Trusted by the U.S. Navy and Federal Agencies, as well as large prime contractors and small businesses' — those primes are private companies, which is why sells_outside_government is yes, but it is a federal-supply-chain relationship, not a commercial market. Our 'EMS' category captures only the fire/EMS side.

name: Rhombus Systems
buyer: Any organization with buildings to secure — retail, manufacturing, healthcare, finance and banking, hotels and hospitality, commercial real estate, construction, storage and warehouse, gyms, places of worship — alongside education (Middlebury Community Schools, Jesuit High School, Los Angeles Film School) and government (City of Sacramento, South Mississippi Housing Authority).
note: Broad-market cloud video security and access control, not a school-safety specialist. The site's own industries menu runs to fourteen verticals of which only Education and Government are public. The government page names small public buyers — Ventura County Air Pollution, Beaver County Tourism, Big Fork Water and Sewer, Village of Palm Springs FL, Dawsonville GA, City of Centerville — and generically targets 'city halls', 'courthouses', 'police stations' and 'fire departments'; a City of Sacramento case study exists too. FINDING: our 'School Safety' category is too narrow. K-12 is a genuine and heavily marketed segment (many school-security blog posts, campus-safety events, FETC), but it is one vertical among many in a company that sells just as hard to retail and manufacturing.

name: Objective Corporation
buyer: Government first — city and regional councils, state and national agencies and regulators (Tauranga City Council, Redland City Council, Salford City Council, Queensland Police, NSW Premier and Cabinet, Scottish Government, Welsh Government, IP Australia, Land Information New Zealand, Wage Inspectorate Victoria) — plus a separate financial-services line sold to investment, fund and asset managers (HUB24, Future Fund) and other regulated companies.
note: Majority public sector, but genuinely not exclusively: the Objective Keystone line is sold to 'Investment, Fund and Asset Managers' and to 'financial services companies and regulated entities worldwide', with solutions for investment reporting, product disclosure, design and distribution obligations and ESG disclosure. ResMed (healthcare manufacturer) also appears as a customer. FINDING for the board: this is an Australian company and nearly every named customer is Australian, New Zealand or UK — councils, state governments, national regulators. The site lists a North America region alongside Australia, NZ, Singapore and the UK, but no US state or local customer is named on the pages I read, so US SLED presence looks thin. Our 'Permitting & Licensing' category matches real product lines (planning and building solutions, statutory planning, electronic plan review, licensing) but the company is much wider than that — records management, information governance and regulatory tech.

name: Nearmap
buyer: Aerial imagery and property-data subscriptions sold to local, state and federal government agencies (City of Grapevine, City of Sioux Falls, Oklahoma County, Village of Huntley, City of Southfield, Eastvale) and, in equal measure, to P&C insurers, architecture/engineering/construction firms, telecom, utilities, solar, roofing and real estate companies.
note: Their government page names seven municipal/county customers by name and quotes a City of Grapevine GIS Manager; the homepage claims "1,500 government agencies worldwide." But government is one of ten industries on their industries page - Insurance, AECO, Telecommunications, Roofing, Utilities, Solar, Real Estate, Property Services and Transportation are the rest, and the homepage brags that "All 10 of the top 10 P&C carriers choose Nearmap." So genuinely dual-market, not a govtech pure-play. Category flag: our record files them under Strategy & Performance, but the site sells aerial imagery, AI feature detection and GIS basemaps - a mapping/imagery product, closer to GIS than to strategy or performance management.

name: Seneca
buyer: Autonomous fire-suppression drone systems sold to fire agencies (Aspen Fire, San Bernardino County Fire, San Mateo County) and alongside them to real estate developers, HOAs and utilities protecting private property.
note: One sentence on their site does all the work: "Seneca works with fire agencies, real estate developers, HOAs, and utilities to protect properties and ecosystems from destructive fires." Public side is real and named - endorsement quotes from the Aspen Fire chief and the San Bernardino County Fire chief, plus CALFIRE and a San Mateo County recruit academy. Private side is equally explicit, so the non-government answer is a clear yes rather than a guess. Other names on the page (Palantir, Watch Duty, Convective Capital, Red Sky Summit) read as partners and investors, not buyers.

name: PayIt
buyer: State and local government agencies only - city and county treasurers, tax assessors and finance directors, state DMVs and conservation/natural-resources departments, court clerks and municipal utility departments.
note: The cleanest record in this batch. Site's own words: "PayIt is a customer experience and payments platform for state and local government." Named customers are all public - Harris County Tax Assessor-Collector, North Carolina DMV, Minnesota DNR, Missouri Department of Conservation, Arkansas Game and Fish Commission, Guilford County NC, City of Grand Rapids MI, City of Columbia MO, and the Kansas iKan state system. Not one commercial buyer appears anywhere on the page. Matches our Procurement & Payments category exactly.

name: Securly
buyer: K-12 school districts - named district customers include Wichita Public Schools, Elgin School District U-46 (IL), Sheboygan Area School District (WI), Howard-Suamico School District (WI), Everett Area School District (PA) and Massac Unit School District #1 (IL).
note: Homepage and about page both frame the entire business as K-12: "27,000+ Schools," "20M+ Students supported," "K-12 schools keep their students safe." Every named customer is a public school district, which is a public buyer, so sells_outside_government is no. One thing worth flagging rather than hiding: Securly Home is a parent-facing app, and parents are not government. I tried the parents page and the Securly Home product page to see whether parents pay directly and neither states who pays - the product is described as controlling "your child's school device," i.e. reaching parents through the district's deployment rather than as a retail purchase. I did not find a consumer price anywhere on the site, so I am not counting parents as a separate buyer.

name: Acusensus
buyer: State and local traffic-enforcement agencies - North Carolina State Highway Patrol, Arkansas DOT, the State of Connecticut, South Lake Minnetonka Police Department, plus programs in Kentucky and Georgia; internationally the New South Wales and Queensland governments and Suffolk Police in the UK.
note: Their US page names public agencies and nothing else: "North Carolina State Highway Patrol engaged Acusensus in a state-wide Commercial Motor Vehicle (CMV) enforcement program," a Connecticut "five-year agreement... to deliver a state-wide automated speed enforcement program," and the Arkansas Speed work-zone program with ARDOT. They also say they have deployed "in 20 states through demonstrations, pilot programs, or contractual engagements." Buyers skew state-level (highway patrols and DOTs) with at least one municipal police department; no commercial customer appears anywhere. Good fit for our Streets category.

name: GameChanger
buyer: Youth sports families and volunteer coaches - the app is free for coaches and team staff, and parents, guardians, family members and fans pay a consumer subscription starting at $3.33/month.
note: This is a consumer subscription business, not a public-sector one. Their own FAQ: "All GameChanger features are completely free for Coaches and Staff to use for their team" and "For families who want more, additional features for Parents/Guardians, Family Members, and Fans... are available with a monthly or annual subscription starting as low as $3.33/month." The organizations page talks about leagues, tournaments and travel orgs and about admins scheduling games, but names no buyer type at all - no parks and recreation department, no school district, no high school. Named affiliations (MLB, Little League, USA Baseball, USA Softball) are private and nonprofit governing bodies, not government. I am leaving sells_to_gov at unclear rather than no because municipal rec leagues plainly use the app and nothing on the site rules that out - but the site itself never names a public buyer, and the revenue clearly comes from families. Worth a second look before this stays on a SLED board under Youth Sports & Leagues.

name: Selux
buyer: Architectural and street lighting sold into public projects (Rittenhouse Square Park, East River State Park, Lincoln Park Long Beach, Denver International Airport, Kona International Airport, Vancouver Fraser Port Authority, White Plains Station) and into private commercial work (T-Mobile CSOC, Heineken Headquarters, Pokemon office, Cabana Bay Beach Resort, Gordon Ramsay Steak).
note: www.selux.com redirects to www.selux.us for the US site; the project gallery there is the real evidence. Public projects are abundant and specific - city parks, two airports, a port authority, a transit station, plus college campuses (Wellesley College, Emily Carr University, Western Technical College) - and they market Smart City Ready poles and a "Lighting for Education" line, with Buy American positioning that reads as written for public procurement. But corporate offices, a resort and a restaurant are on the same page, so the commercial half is not a guess. One practical caveat for the board: they are a luminaire manufacturer selling through specifiers, lighting designers and distributors, so the public agency is often the project owner rather than the direct purchaser.

name: PayNearMe
buyer: Mostly commercial billers - auto and consumer lenders, credit unions, buy-here-pay-here dealers, mortgage servicers, iGaming and sports betting operators, and law firms; named customers include OneMain Financial, United Auto Credit, CAR Financial Services, Northwoods Automotive and FanDuel. Their one public-sector vertical is tolling, where The Toll Roads of Orange County is the named customer.
note: paynearme.com redirects to home.paynearme.com. The site lists seven verticals and six are plainly commercial: Auto & Consumer Lending, Credit Unions, iGaming, Buy Here Pay Here, Mortgage Servicing and Law Firms. There is no government vertical. The only SLED-relevant one is Tolling, which addresses "toll authorities" and "toll operators" and features The Toll Roads of Orange County - operated by a public joint-powers toll authority, which our own rules count as a public buyer, though the page itself never calls it government. That is why I set sells_to_gov to yes but confidence to medium: the public read depends on knowing what The Toll Roads is, not on the site saying so. Worth flagging against our Procurement & Payments category - this is a consumer-finance payments company with a tolling side, not a government payments platform like PayIt.

name: NAVBLUE
buyer: Airlines and aircraft operators - named customers on the live site are Corsair, Japan Airlines, Hong Kong Air Cargo and AirAsia. No airport, air navigation service provider or government aviation authority is named as a buyer anywhere I could read.
note: Important change: www.navblue.aero no longer serves its own site. Every URL I tried, the root and individual product and news pages, 301-redirects to www.skywise.com - NAVBLUE has been merged into Skywise, "an Airbus digital services company," and the brand is being absorbed. So the website in our record is effectively dead and should be updated. Reading the surviving site, the only customers named are commercial airlines, and the positioning line is about "all operators, including those with non-Airbus fleets" - operators, not agencies. NAVBLUE's older boilerplate described serving "airlines, airports and Air Navigation Service Providers," which would be SLED-relevant since US airport and port authorities are public, but I only saw that in a search snippet and could not confirm it on any page the site still serves, so I am not treating it as evidence. Category flag: our Airfield & Operations label fits the old airport/ATM business, not the airline flight-operations software the live site actually sells.

name: DEVNET Inc
buyer: County government offices and municipal assessors - named customers are McLean County IL IT, Piatt County IL Clerk and Recorder, Bond County IL Clerk and Recorder, Morgan County IL GIS, the Wauwatosa WI Assessor, and the Oakland County MI Treasurer.
note: A government-only vendor. Their Edge platform page says "One solution to serve government" and describes opening records to "the public, local offices, outside agencies and partner organizations." Every named customer across the homepage and testimonials page is a county office or a city assessor, and the product line - CAMA and assessment administration, tax billing and collection, records management, permitting and zoning, tax bill printing and mailing - only makes sense for a county courthouse. No commercial buyer appears anywhere. Mild category note: we file them under Finance & ERP, which is defensible for the tax billing and collection side, but the core of the product is property assessment and land records rather than general government ERP.
